generatedFrom: Den art direction v2 — background, display furniture, treasures and Momo are separate composited layers
purpose: Brief for the den artwork. The den is assembled from separate layers so generated environment art never has to hit pixel-exact shelf coordinates. Backgrounds communicate the same home improving from run-down shelter to palace, while display furniture, treasures and Momo remain crisp, controllable overlays.

style.medium: Painted digital illustration matching the rest of Matemostri: soft airbrushed rendering with real light and shadow, not flat vector art and not a photo.
style.palette: Warm gold light against plum-purple, with sage green, dusty pink and cream accents. Materials become richer as the den improves.
style.mood: Cosy and magical, never dark or spooky. The progression must read as objectively better living conditions: run-down -> cosy -> luxurious -> palace.
style.continuity: All four backgrounds are the SAME physical room. Keep the same major walls, openings, floor perspective and overall camera. Each stage repairs, enlarges, finishes and enriches what was already there. Do not turn stages into different themes or biomes.
style.visualHierarchy: Momo and the child's treasures are the heroes. Background detail must be restrained. Use broad calm wall/floor shapes, keep small props mainly at the perimeter, and avoid decorative objects that compete with or resemble collectibles. Later dens become richer through better materials, architecture, light and a few larger furnishings, not through filling every surface with clutter.
style.framing: Clean rectangular full-bleed scene. No parchment border or vignette frame. The app supplies its own rounded card.
doNotIncludeInBackground: Shelves, plinths, cabinets or other collectible display furniture
Any treasures or objects that could be mistaken for collectible rewards
Dense shelves of books, bottles, trinkets or tiny props
Strong focal objects in the Momo or treasure-display zones

coordinateSystem.note: Export backgrounds at exact 1.6:1. The game composites display furniture, treasures and Momo over the background. Keep important background architecture away from the outermost 12px because the card rounds the corners.

backgrounds.name: Run-down hideaway
backgrounds.artDirection: The original humble room: weathered walls, rough floor, simple sleeping nook, one warm light, signs of age and repair needed. Charming and safe, but clearly poor. Keep it sparse.
backgrounds.progression: Baseline architecture for every later background.

backgrounds.name: Cosy home
backgrounds.artDirection: Exactly the same room repaired and cared for: sound floor, comfortable sleeping area, rug, curtains, warmer lighting, a plant and a few homely touches. Noticeably better than level 1, still simple and uncluttered.

backgrounds.name: Beautiful magical home
backgrounds.artDirection: Same room now genuinely luxurious: fine carved wood, richer fabrics, larger/brighter window treatment, elegant architectural finishing, subtle magical glow and better furnishings. It must be obviously more desirable than level 2 without changing theme. Preserve generous empty display space.

backgrounds.name: Guardian palace
backgrounds.artDirection: The same humble home transformed into a small magical palace: polished stone or marble integrated with the original wood, taller architecture, refined gold details, grand windows, banners and beautiful light. Spectacular but compositionally calm so the complete treasure collection dominates the room.
backgrounds.progression: Palace-level architecture and materials, not more clutter.

momo.note: Keep this central footprint low-detail in every background.

displayZone.note: Keep this zone relatively calm. Display furniture is composited here separately and may evolve as the den improves. Exact shelf surfaces and treasure slots belong to the display asset/layout data, not the generated background.

displayFurniture.purpose: Separate transparent WebP artwork placed over the den background. It carries all pixel-exact surfaces on which treasures sit.
displayFurniture.artDirection: Furniture should visibly improve with the den while remaining part of the same home's design language: rough/simple -> finished wood -> carved luxury -> ornate palace display.

levels.brief: A very small rough display solution appropriate to the run-down hideaway. Final slot count should be decided with Collectibles v2 game logic before production.
Simple but well-made wooden treasure display.
Elegant carved treasure display with richer materials.
Ornate palace-quality display for all eight collectible families.

displayFurniture.implementationNote: Do not bake display furniture into den-N.webp. Code owns its position and treasure slot coordinates. Define final slot counts/centres alongside Collectibles v2 implementation, then export the display art to fit those coordinates exactly.

collectibles.rendering: Separate artwork, composited above the display furniture. Each collectible needs a clear silhouette and stronger local contrast than the den background.
collectibles.v2Plan: 8 families x 3 progression tiers = 24 specimens. Replays can earn duplicates/upgrades, but the den should show a curated/best representative rather than filling the scene with duplicate clutter.

productionWorkflow: Approve den-1 background architecture first, with no display furniture, collectibles or Momo.
Generate/paint den-2, den-3 and den-4 as upgrades of that exact same room, keeping backgrounds intentionally restrained.
Implement/confirm Collectibles v2 slot counts and display behaviour.
Create one transparent display-furniture asset per den level against the exact code geometry.
Create the 24 transparent collectible specimen assets.
Composite in the game and adjust overlay coordinates in layout data, never by regenerating a background to chase pixel positions.
Ship WebP assets. PNG files must not be added to assets.
